drugs.name: maropitant (injectable)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication

Injectable acute vomiting (dog+cat, label): 1 mg/kg SC or IV (IV over 1–2 min) once daily up to 5 consecutive days. Dogs: SC from 2 months; SC/IV from 4 months. Cats: FDA-approved vomiting treatment from 4 months at 1 mg/kg SC or IV up to 5 days. (Plumb 10th pp. 799–802.)
Dog PO acute vomiting (tablet label): 2 mg/kg PO once daily; min age 2 months; 5 days if 2–7 months, until vomiting ceases if older. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)

Dog PO motion sickness (tablet label): 8 mg/kg PO once daily up to 2 consecutive days; min age 4 months; empty stomach or small amount of food — do not feed full meal prior to travel. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)

Cat PO/SC extra-label: 1 mg/kg SC or PO (Plumb pp. 801–802, flagged extra-label). iCatCare CKD 2026 Table 4: 1 mg/kg SC, IV or PO q24h for nausea/vomiting. Do NOT use Plumb CKD ‘4 mg/cat (NOT mg/kg)’ as mg/kg. Cerenia dog tablets in cats = extra-label vs dog tablet licence; injectable labelled for cats.
Active vomiting: injectable preferred to ensure full dose received. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)

Product strengths (Plumb Dosage Forms p. 802): Cerenia® injectable 10 mg/mL; tablets 16, 24, 60, 160 mg. Hospital stock commonly Prevomax 10 mg/mL inj and Cerenia 16/24 mg tabs (stock selection among labelled strengths).
2. Major adverse effects
Generally well tolerated; allergic reactions rare. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
SC: injection-site pain/swelling; refrigerating injection may reduce pain. (Plumb 10th pp. 799–801.)
Dogs at motion-sickness oral dose: pretravel vomiting, hypersalivation most common. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
Other dog AEs: depression/lethargy, anorexia, diarrhea, anaphylaxis/anaphylactoid (incl. facial swelling), ataxia, tremors, fever, dyspnea, collapse, sedation, convulsions. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
Cat AEs: depression/lethargy, anorexia, injection-site pain, hypersalivation, dyspnea, ataxia, fever, recumbency, vomiting, panting, convulsion, muscle tremors. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
IV under isoflurane: further BP decrease; hypotension with acepromazine premed reported. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
QT prolongation (cardiac K-channel blockade). (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
Ca-channel blockers (amlodipine, diltiazem, verapamil): UK label — should not use concomitantly. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
CYP3A inhibitors (amiodarone, diltiazem, cimetidine, erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole): may reduce maropitant metabolism. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
CYP2D inhibitors (cimetidine, fluoxetine, terbinafine): may reduce maropitant metabolism. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
Highly protein-bound drugs (valproic acid, oral anticoagulants, NSAIDs, salicylates, sulfonamides, sulfonylureas): theoretical displacement — monitor. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
QT-prolonging agents (cisapride, domperidone, quinidine, sotalol): avoid — increased QT risk. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
Pantoprazole: precipitation reported in same IV line; UK label — do not mix with other products in same syringe. (Plumb 10th p. 802.)
Drug interactions not thoroughly investigated. (Plumb 10th pp. 800–801.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients
Safe use not evaluated in GI obstruction or toxin ingestion. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Hepatic dysfunction: caution; consider 50% dose reduction. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Underlying cardiac disease with antiarrhythmics: safe use not reported (QT concern). (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Breeding/pregnant/lactating: safety not established — maternal benefits vs offspring risks. (Plumb 10th p. 800.)
Motion-sickness dose caution in puppies <11 weeks (bone marrow hypoplasia signal); not seen at ≥16 weeks. (Plumb 10th pp. 799–800.) Client info: do not give to puppies <8 weeks. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
Dog tablets acute vomiting: ≥2 months. (Plumb 10th pp. 799, 801.)
Dog tablets motion sickness: ≥4 months. (Plumb 10th pp. 799, 801.)
Dog injectable: SC ≥2 months; SC/IV ≥4 months; chemo/emetogenic prevention ≥4 months. (Plumb 10th pp. 800–801.)
Cat injectable label: ≥4 months. (Plumb 10th pp. 799, 801–802.)
Extra-label cat PO 1 mg/kg: no separate Plumb minimum age beyond injectable label context; iCatCare Table 4 does not add a different age floor in prior verified cite.
6. Any special instructions
Refrigerate injectable and inject promptly to reduce SC pain. (Plumb 10th pp. 799–801.)
Motion sickness: ~2 h before travel with small amount of food (not full meal); do not wrap pills tightly in food snacks. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)
IV over 1–2 minutes. (Plumb 10th pp. 800–801.)
Dog PO dose higher than SC due to lower oral bioavailability. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Feeding status does not affect bioavailability (PK). (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Give before chemotherapeutic for best prevention of chemo-associated vomiting. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
If vomiting persists, re-evaluate cause. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Crushing tablets: Not stated in available sources.
Splitting: Client info allows fractions (half, quarter); wrap remaining split tablet in foil. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)
Halved tablets out of blister: no potency loss over 48 h testing (European stability note). (Plumb 10th p. 801.)
Tablet scoring marks: Not stated in available sources.
8. Others
Brands in Plumb: Cerenia®, Prevomax®. (Plumb 10th p. 801.)
NK-1 antagonist; peripheral or central emesis. (Plumb 10th p. 799.)
Keep Plumb CKD 4 mg/cat (NOT mg/kg) separate from 1 mg/kg regimens; prefer iCatCare 1 mg/kg for mg/kg display.
Human skin/eye exposure precautions. (Plumb 10th pp. 800–801.)

drugs.name: doxycycline (tablets)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication

Respiratory (URI/CIRDC/bronchitis) dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h (one pattern). B. bronchiseptica, Mycoplasma spp., C. felis (cats); hyclate or monohydrate OK; >4 weeks without enamel discoloration. (ISCAID respiratory 2017 Table 2.)
UTI reserved dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO every 12 h only; low urine excretion; reserved for resistant pathogens. (ISCAID UTI 2019.)
Canine pyoderma second-choice (dogs): 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h; hyclate=monohydrate; BC/AST; test doxycycline specifically. (ISCAID pyoderma 2025 Table 15.)
Plumb general extra-label support (not display source): dogs/cats susceptible infections / acute respiratory often 5 mg/kg PO q12h or 10 mg/kg PO q24h. (Plumb 10th pp. 436–437.)
2. Major adverse effects
Most common oral AEs dogs/cats: vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia; food may help GI without major absorption loss. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Esophagitis and esophageal strictures — especially cats. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435–436.)
Increased ALT/ALP in up to ~40% dogs and ~19% cats; often not clinically significant in dogs. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Monohydrate may be less GI/esophagitis risk than hyclate — comparative animal data lacking. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Class notes: photosensitivity; rarely hepatotoxicity/blood dyscrasias (humans). (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Do not give IM or SC (injection-site AEs) — hospital scope PO. (Plumb 10th p. 433.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
Al/Ca/Mg oral products: chelation ↓ absorption — separate ≥1–2 h. (Plumb 10th pp. 435–436.)
Oral iron: preferably 3 h before or 2 h after tetracycline. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Zinc; bismuth subsalicylate; kaolin/pectin: separate 1–2 h. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Sucralfate: ↓ doxycycline exposure in dogs; OK if sucralfate 2 h after doxycycline. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole): may ↓ oral bioavailability. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Phenobarbital: may ↓ half-life/concentrations. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Ascorbic acid: may ↓ efficacy. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Warfarin: may need anticoagulant adjustment. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Penicillins/cephalosporins/aminoglycosides: theoretical bacteriostatic interference. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)

Client: avoid multivitamins/Ca/antacids/laxatives 2 h before/after; food without iron or dairy for stomach upset. (Plumb 10th p. 437.) Human PK: dairy/high-fat meal may reduce absorption ~20% only. (Plumb 10th p. 434.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients
Hypersensitivity to doxycycline. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Pregnancy/pediatrics: tetracycline class fetal skeletal/teeth risks — last half pregnancy only if benefits outweigh; doxycycline much less likely than older tetracyclines. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435.)
Nursing: excreted in milk — dams should not nurse; benefits vs risks. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Significant hepatic dysfunction (dogs): use with caution. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Renal insufficiency: CAN be used (does not accumulate) — not a contraindication. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435.)
Long-term: superinfection risk; photosensitivity — limit sun in thin/light coats. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
ISCAID respiratory Table 2: kittens and puppies >4 weeks of age without enamel discoloration.

Plumb: bone/teeth abnormalities possible but much less likely than other tetracyclines; weigh benefits vs risks in pregnant/pediatric animals — no separate numeric earliest age in weeks for dogs/cats in opened monograph beyond that. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435.)
6. Any special instructions
Cats: never dry-pill; follow with ≥5 mL water or food (Plumb); ISCAID: lubricant + water / pill treat / ≥2 mL liquid / food. (Plumb 10th pp. 435–437; ISCAID respiratory 2017; ISCAID UTI 2019.)
Moist treat or small liquid so dose reaches stomach — especially cats. (Plumb 10th p. 437.)
GI upset: small food without iron or dairy; separate antacids/Ca/multivitamins/laxatives by 2 h. (Plumb 10th p. 437.)
Complete full course unless directed otherwise. (Plumb 10th p. 437.)
Prefer commercial oral liquid/suspension vs unstable compounded aqueous suspensions. (Plumb 10th p. 438 compounding.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Explicit crush/split scored-tablet recommendation: Not stated in available sources.
Compounded slurry (eg ‘triple fish’) listed as cat administration alternative. (Plumb 10th pp. 436–437.)

Tablets mixed with water/foods (milk, pudding, yogurt, applesauce, jellies) lose >10% potency after 24 h. Compounded aqueous suspensions: refrigerate, protect from light, use within 7 days. (Plumb 10th p. 438.)
Hospital paste: same mg/kg as tablets; avoids dry-pilling solids — form preference not dose change. (ISCAID; hospital stock.)
8. Others
No FDA-approved systemic veterinary doxycycline products — typically extra-label systemic use. (Plumb 10th pp. 434, 438.)
Preferred tetracycline in azotemic patients when a tetracycline is indicated. (Plumb 10th p. 434.)
MDR1 dogs: no dose alteration recommended (WSU CPL). (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Hospital paste ≠ assurance of compounded-aqueous stability — follow Plumb compounding caveats if mixed extemporaneously.

drugs.name: doxycycline (paste)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication

Respiratory (URI/CIRDC/bronchitis) dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h (one pattern). B. bronchiseptica, Mycoplasma spp., C. felis (cats); hyclate or monohydrate OK; >4 weeks without enamel discoloration. (ISCAID respiratory 2017 Table 2.)
UTI reserved dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO every 12 h only; low urine excretion; reserved for resistant pathogens. (ISCAID UTI 2019.)
Canine pyoderma second-choice (dogs): 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h; hyclate=monohydrate; BC/AST; test doxycycline specifically. (ISCAID pyoderma 2025 Table 15.)
Plumb general extra-label support (not display source): dogs/cats susceptible infections / acute respiratory often 5 mg/kg PO q12h or 10 mg/kg PO q24h. (Plumb 10th pp. 436–437.)
2. Major adverse effects
Most common oral AEs dogs/cats: vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia; food may help GI without major absorption loss. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Esophagitis and esophageal strictures — especially cats. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435–436.)
Increased ALT/ALP in up to ~40% dogs and ~19% cats; often not clinically significant in dogs. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Monohydrate may be less GI/esophagitis risk than hyclate — comparative animal data lacking. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Class notes: photosensitivity; rarely hepatotoxicity/blood dyscrasias (humans). (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Do not give IM or SC (injection-site AEs) — hospital scope PO. (Plumb 10th p. 433.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
Al/Ca/Mg oral products: chelation ↓ absorption — separate ≥1–2 h. (Plumb 10th pp. 435–436.)
Oral iron: preferably 3 h before or 2 h after tetracycline. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Zinc; bismuth subsalicylate; kaolin/pectin: separate 1–2 h. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Sucralfate: ↓ doxycycline exposure in dogs; OK if sucralfate 2 h after doxycycline. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole): may ↓ oral bioavailability. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Phenobarbital: may ↓ half-life/concentrations. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Ascorbic acid: may ↓ efficacy. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Warfarin: may need anticoagulant adjustment. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)
Penicillins/cephalosporins/aminoglycosides: theoretical bacteriostatic interference. (Plumb 10th p. 436.)

Client: avoid multivitamins/Ca/antacids/laxatives 2 h before/after; food without iron or dairy for stomach upset. (Plumb 10th p. 437.) Human PK: dairy/high-fat meal may reduce absorption ~20% only. (Plumb 10th p. 434.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients
Hypersensitivity to doxycycline. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Pregnancy/pediatrics: tetracycline class fetal skeletal/teeth risks — last half pregnancy only if benefits outweigh; doxycycline much less likely than older tetracyclines. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435.)
Nursing: excreted in milk — dams should not nurse; benefits vs risks. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Significant hepatic dysfunction (dogs): use with caution. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
Renal insufficiency: CAN be used (does not accumulate) — not a contraindication. (Plumb 10th pp. 433, 435.)
Long-term: superinfection risk; photosensitivity — limit sun in thin/light coats. (Plumb 10th p. 435.)
